headline: Linux creator Linus Torvalds has posted a kernel patch written with an AI coding assistant, aimed at removing a slowdown when many processor cores read the same file.
score_reason: Lowered from 6 to 4: the patches date from about 10 to 12 Oct and were widely reported then, and the 23-fold figure differs from the roughly threefold other outlets reported.
importance_line: Linux kernel developers and the many organisations that run Linux are affected first, but the 23-fold figure comes from a synthetic test, ZDNET and Linuxiac reported about threefold in the main test they described, and the patches are not yet in the main kernel.
summary: Tom's Hardware reports that Linus Torvalds, the creator and lead maintainer of the Linux kernel, has posted what it calls his first AI-assisted patch, a fix for a slowdown that occurs when many processor cores read the same file, and that he claims it ran 23 times faster in a synthetic benchmark, a figure he says real workloads would not match. The work was first reported around 12 Oct 2026, when our edition of that day carried Phoronix's report that Torvalds was building a kernel improvement with Anthropic's Claude Code; the patch sits on a development branch, not in the main kernel.
notes: Read Tom's Hardware in full (16 Oct). Context read at ZDNET (13 Oct) and Linuxiac (12 Oct): Torvalds's own commit text, dated 10 Oct per Linuxiac, says the code, tests and review were done with Claude Code under his direction; they report about 10 million to 30-33 million reads per second (about threefold) in the main eight-thread test and a branch outside mainline Linux 7.3-rc6 as of 13 Oct. Tom's Hardware's 23x figure could not be matched to those numbers; XenoSpectrum (17 Oct) reports a race condition found in review, but its page was blocked, so that is not used.
